hints: Think about how many Plasmodium species infect humans - you have been given two names already, so recall what other species names you have seen linked to malaria.
walkthrough:
Recall the human malaria parasites**
There are five Plasmodium species that infect humans. The stem already gives you P. vivax and P. falciparum, so you need one different one you have learned.

Give the correct name**
P. ovale and P. malariae are both accepted. Write the full genus plus species, e.g. Plasmodium ovale, with correct spelling.
Final answer: Plasmodium ovale / Plasmodium malariae

hints: Start by thinking where this haemoglobin normally works - what fluid is it in and what conditions does it experience inside the human body?
Now link that to the experiment - what exact values would mimic the body, and why would changing pH or temperature change the curve?
walkthrough:
Mimic the body**
Fig. 5.1 is for normal adult haemoglobin in humans, so the lab solution must copy the body. That means blood pH of about pH 7.4 and body temperature of about $37 ^\circ\text{C}$.

Why standardise to those values**
Haemoglobin loading and unloading of oxygen is very sensitive to pH and temperature. A lower pH or higher temperature lowers affinity. So researchers fix them at body values to get a valid normal curve for comparison.
Final answer: Use conditions occurring in the body / blood / plasma: pH approx. 7.4 and $37 ^\circ\text{C}$; as oxygen uptake / affinity of haemoglobin is affected by pH and temperature.

hints: Picture Fig. 5.1 moving to the right - at any fixed partial pressure on the x-axis, would the curve now be higher or lower on the y-axis?
Translate that up-or-down change into the key word affinity - what does a right shift tell you about how strongly haemoglobin holds oxygen?
Now apply that to the two places in the body - high partial pressure in the lungs for loading, and low partial pressure in respiring tissues for unloading.
walkthrough:
What right shift means**
A shift to the right means at any given partial pressure of oxygen the percentage saturation is lower. In other words the affinity of haemoglobin for oxygen has decreased.

Effect in the lungs**
In the lungs the partial pressure is high and haemoglobin should load to near 95-97% as in Fig. 5.1. With lower affinity, loading is more difficult and a higher partial pressure would be needed to reach the same saturation.

Effect in the tissues**
In respiring tissues the partial pressure is low. Because affinity is lower, haemoglobin gives up oxygen more easily, so more oxygen is released at any one partial pressure. That is unloading is enhanced, but loading was poorer.

Final answer: Affinity of haemoglobin for oxygen decreases; lower percentage saturation at any partial pressure, so more difficult to load oxygen in lungs and higher partial pressure needed for same saturation; oxygen released more readily / more released at same partial pressure in respiring tissues.

hints: Start with the job - carrying oxygen in blood through the very narrowest vessels - what size must the cell be to get through capillaries and what does that do to flow?
Next think about the classic shape you can see under the microscope - how does being biconcave rather than spherical help with surface area and diffusion?
Then think about what is missing inside a mature mammalian red cell compared to most other cells - what organelles are lost?
For each feature, finish the link to function - more space for what, less use of what, and easier squeezing through what?
walkthrough:
Small and flexible to use capillaries**
A red cell is about $6-8 \mu\text{m}$ in diameter, so it just fits through a capillary lumen. Cells pass through one by one in single file, which slows blood flow and gives maximum time for oxygen uptake and keeps diffusion distance very short. The cell surface membrane is flexible so the cell can deform and squeeze through.

Biconcave for fast gas exchange**
The biconcave disc shape gives a large surface area to volume ratio compared to a sphere, so there is more area for oxygen to diffuse in. The centre is very thin, so the diffusion distance from the surface to haemoglobin inside is very short.

No nucleus or mitochondria to carry more and waste less**
Mature red cells have no nucleus and no mitochondria. That leaves more space inside for haemoglobin. Having no mitochondria is especially helpful because the cell itself does not use up by respiration any of the oxygen it is transporting.

Final answer: Diameter $6-8 \mu\text{m}$ to pass through capillaries single file, slowing flow and reducing diffusion distance for oxygen uptake; flexible cell surface membrane to deform / squeeze through capillaries; biconcave shape giving increased surface area to volume ratio for uptake and short diffusion distance to haemoglobin; no nucleus / no mitochondria giving more space for haemoglobin and no mitochondria so no oxygen used in respiration.
